'''''Buddleja asiatica''''', also known as '''dogtail''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile/BUAS|title=USDA Plants Database|website=plants.usda.gov|access-date=November 8, 2025}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the figwort family, ''[[Scrophulariaceae]]''.<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |url= https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:545686-1 |title= Buddleja asiatica Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=July 18, 2025}}</ref><ref name=COL>{{cite web |url= https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/NMYY |title= Buddleja asiatica Lour. |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=n.d. |website=Catalogue of Life |publisher=Species 2000 |access-date=July 18, 2025}}</ref> It grows in open woodland at elevations < 2,800 m  either as understorey scrub, or as a small tree.<ref name=Stuart>Stuart, D. (2006). ''Buddlejas''. Plant Collector Guide. Timber Press, Oregon, USA. {{ISBN|978-0-88192-688-0}}</ref> First described by [[João de Loureiro|Loureiro]] in 1790, ''B. asiatica'' was introduced to the [[UK]] in 1874, and accorded the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]] [[Award of Garden Merit]] (record 675) in 1993.<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/28038/i-Buddleja-asiatica-i/Details| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Buddleja asiatica''| access-date=12 January 2018}}</ref><ref name=Hillier>Hillier Nurseries (1977). ''Hilliers' Manual of Trees & Shrubs''. David & Charles, Newton Abbot. {{ISBN|0-7153-6744-7}}</ref> It is highly [[invasive species|invasive]] in [[Hawaii]], [[Guam]], and the [[Northern Mariana Islands]].<ref name=HEAR>{{cite web|title=Buddleja asiatica: info from PIER (PIER species info)|url=http://www.hear.org/pier/species/buddleja_asiatica.htm|publisher=Hawaii Ecosystems At Risk|access-date=12 March 2018}}</ref>

==Description==
''Buddleja asiatica'' can grow < 7 m tall in the wild. The leaves are usually narrowly [[leaf shape|lanceolate]] to [[leaf shape|ovoid]], < 30 cm long, attached by [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s 15 mm long, to branches round in section. The sweetly scented flowers are usually white, occasionally pale violet, and borne in late winter at the ends of the long, lax branches in slender panicles, the size of which can vary widely according to source.<ref name=Stuart/> [[Ploidy]]: 2''n'' = 38 ([[ploidy|diploid]]).<ref name=Chen>Chen, G, Sun, W-B, & Sun, H. (2007). Ploidy variation in Buddleja L. (Buddlejaceae) in the Sino - Himalayan region and its biogeographical implications. ''Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society.'' 2007, 154, 305 – 312. The Linnean Society of London.</ref>

==Distribution==
This somewhat tender [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] is native to [[Assam]], [[Bangladesh]], [[Borneo]], [[Cambodia]], [[China]] (North-Central, South-Central and Southeast), East and West [[Himalaya]], [[Hainan]], [[India]], [[Java]], [[Laos]], the [[Lesser Sunda Islands]], [[Malaysia]], the [[Maluku Islands]], the [[Mariana Islands]], [[Myanmar]], [[Nepal]], [[New Guinea]], [[Pakistan]], the [[Philippines]], [[Sulawesi]], [[Sumatra]], [[Taiwan]], [[Thailand]], [[Tibet]], [[Vietnam]].<ref name=POWO/> It is an [[introduced species]] in the East Aegean Islands, [[Hawaii]], and [[Vanuatu]].<ref name=POWO/>

==Cultivation==
''Buddleja asiatica'' is not completely hardy in the [[UK]], but can be grown reliably against a south-facing wall in coastal areas of the south and west, where it tolerates temperatures down to around {{convert|0|C|F}}. A specimen is grown under glass by [[Longstock Park]] Nursery, near [[Stockbridge, Hampshire]], one of the four [[NCCPG]] national collection holders.
[[Hardiness zone|Hardiness]]: RHS H3,<ref name = RHSPF /> [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] zones 9–10.<ref name=Stuart/> Owing to its wide ecological range, adaptation to disturbed areas, elevation and rainfall tolerance, it readily naturalizes in tropical regions and can become invasive.<ref name = HEAR />

==Uses==
In [[Nepal]] leaves of ''B. asiatica'' are collected as fodder for domesticated animals, and the trunk is cut for firewood. During [[Thami|Thangmi]] wedding rituals, the female relatives of the groom wear necklaces made of the white flower.<ref name=DH>{{cite web|last=Turin|first=Mark|title=ETHNOBOTANICAL NOTES ON THANGMI PLANT NAMES AND THEIR MEDICINAL AND RITUAL USES|url=http://www.digitalhimalaya.com/projectteam/turin/downloads/plant_names.pdf|work=www.digitalhimalaya.com|publisher=www.digitalhimalaya.com|access-date=17 November 2013}}</ref>
